# Physical Lowering and Operator Choice {#sec-physical-lowering}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

A logical operator says *what* to compute. A physical operator says
*how*. The distinction matters because there is usually more than
one way: a join can be hash or nested-loop; an aggregation can be
key-grouped or globally streamed; a memory layout can be row or
columnar. Lowering is the engine's commitment to a particular
*how*.

In NebulaStream, lowering is a phase in `nes-query-compiler/`
called `LowerToPhysicalOperators`. It runs after optimisation and
before pipelining. By the time it finishes, every logical operator
has been replaced by an instance of a physical operator class
that knows how to participate in code generation.

---

## 10.1 The physical operator concept {#sec-physical-concept}

Physical operators, like logical operators, are defined through a
C++20 concept rather than a class hierarchy. The concept lives in
`nes-physical-operators/include/PhysicalOperator.hpp`:

```cpp
// nes-physical-operators/include/PhysicalOperator.hpp
template <typename T>
concept PhysicalOperatorConcept = requires(T op) {
    { op.setup(...) };
    { op.open(...) };
    { op.execute(...) };
    { op.close(...) };
};
```

Four lifecycle methods, executed during code generation:

- **`setup`** — called once at compile time. Allocates per-operator
  state, registers handlers.
- **`open`** — called at the start of each pipeline invocation.
  Initialises per-invocation state.
- **`execute`** — called once per `Record`. The hot path. Most of
  the actual work happens here.
- **`close`** — called at the end of each pipeline invocation.
  Flushes anything pending.

These look like a standard producer/consumer protocol because they
are. NebulaStream's physical operators are essentially Volcano-
style operators with the per-tuple `next()` replaced by a per-batch
`execute(Record)` and the whole protocol expressed at code-
generation time rather than at runtime.

---

## 10.2 The physical operator catalogue {#sec-physical-catalogue}

The classes live in `nes-physical-operators/include/`. The major
ones:

| Logical operator | Physical implementations |
|---|---|
| Source | `SourcePhysicalOperator` |
| Sink | `SinkPhysicalOperator` |
| Selection | `SelectionPhysicalOperator` |
| Projection | `ProjectionPhysicalOperator` |
| Map | `MapPhysicalOperator` |
| Join (hash) | `HJBuildPhysicalOperator` + `HJProbePhysicalOperator` |
| Join (nested-loop) | `NLJBuildPhysicalOperator` + `NLJProbePhysicalOperator` |
| Aggregation | `AggregationBuildPhysicalOperator` + `AggregationProbePhysicalOperator` |

A few observations.

Stateful operators come in pairs — a *build* operator that
accumulates state, and a *probe* operator that emits results. The
two halves run on different sides of a pipeline boundary (Chapter 11)
and communicate through a shared state structure registered during
`setup`. This is the classical streaming-join pattern.

Stateless operators are single classes. A `Selection` is just an
`execute` that calls a predicate; if the predicate returns true,
the record passes; if false, it is dropped.

A `Map` is a pure transformation per field; the implementation is a
thin wrapper that, at code-generation time, emits the field-by-field
arithmetic.

---

## 10.3 The lowering rule registry {#sec-lowering-registry}

Lowering itself is implemented as a *rule registry*. Each logical
operator type has a corresponding lowering rule registered in
`LoweringRuleRegistry`. The rule's job is to take a logical operator
plus context and return a physical operator (or, for stateful
operators, a pair).

The dispatch is in `LowerToPhysicalOperators.cpp`:

```cpp
// nes-query-compiler/src/Phases/LowerToPhysicalOperators.cpp
std::unique_ptr<AbstractLoweringRule>
resolveLoweringRule(const LogicalOperator& logicalOperator,
                    const LoweringRuleRegistryArguments& registryArgument)
{
    if (logicalOperatorName == "Join")
    {
        const auto implementationTraitOpt
            = getTrait<JoinImplementationTypeTrait>(traitSet);
        switch (implementationTrait->implementationType)
        {
            case JoinImplementation::HASH_JOIN:
                return LoweringRuleRegistry::instance()
                           .create("HashJoin", registryArgument);
            case JoinImplementation::NESTED_LOOP_JOIN:
                return LoweringRuleRegistry::instance()
                           .create("NLJoin", registryArgument);
        }
    }
    // ... generic case for other operators
}
```

For a join, the dispatch reads the `JoinImplementationTypeTrait`
attached by `DecideJoinTypesRule` (Chapter 9) and selects the
appropriate physical operator factory by name. For other operators
the dispatch is a single-name lookup.

The registry is the same plugin pattern we will see in detail in
Chapter 13. Its presence here means a third party can add a new
join implementation — say, an interval-join algorithm — by
registering a lowering rule named "IntervalJoin" and updating the
optimiser's join-type decision to choose it. The framework is not
locked.

---

## 10.4 The hash-join lowering, in detail {#sec-hash-join-lower}

A `JoinLogicalOperator` whose trait says `HASH_JOIN` lowers into
*two* physical operators:

```cpp
// nes-physical-operators/include/Join/HashJoin/HJBuildPhysicalOperator.hpp
class HJBuildPhysicalOperator : public StreamJoinBuildPhysicalOperator {
public:
    HJBuildPhysicalOperator(
        OperatorHandlerId operatorHandlerId,
        JoinBuildSideType joinBuildSide,
        std::unique_ptr<TimeFunction> timeFunction,
        const std::shared_ptr<TupleBufferRef>& bufferRef,
        HashMapOptions hashMapOptions);
    void setup(ExecutionContext& executionCtx,
               CompilationContext& compilationContext) const override;
    void execute(ExecutionContext& ctx, Record& record) const override;
};
```

The build operator accepts records from one side of the join and
inserts them into a hash map keyed on the join key. The probe
operator accepts records from the other side and looks them up,
emitting joined records on each match.

The hash map itself is one of the runtime data structures from
`nes-nautilus/`, a JIT-aware container we will examine in Chapter 12.
For now, note that the build's `setup` method registers a handler
that owns the hash map; both build and probe share access to it
through an `OperatorHandlerId`.

The pair-of-operators pattern is also how the build/probe split
introduces a *pipeline boundary*: the build is on one pipeline,
the probe on another, with the hash map mediating between them.
That is the Chapter 11 story.

---

## 10.5 Aggregation: same structure, different state {#sec-aggregation}

Aggregations also lower into a build/probe pair. The build inserts
records into a hash map keyed on the grouping key (or, for global
aggregations, into a single accumulator). The probe walks the hash
map after each window fires and emits one record per group.

The interesting difference from joins is that the aggregation's
hash map values are *partial aggregates*, not records. For
`AVG(speed)`, the value is `(sum, count)`; for `MAX(value)` it is
the running maximum. The aggregation function knows how to
combine a partial aggregate with an incoming value (the
`combine` step) and how to convert a partial aggregate into a
result tuple (the `extract` step).

The actual aggregation classes are in
`nes-physical-operators/include/Aggregation/`. The aggregation
function vocabulary is in
`nes-logical-operators/include/Operators/Windows/Aggregations/` —
SUM, COUNT, MIN, MAX, AVG, plus a generic UDF aggregation slot.

---

## 10.6 What is *not* in the lowering phase {#sec-lower-non-goals}

Several decisions feel like they ought to belong here but do not.

**Code generation** belongs to the next two phases (pipelining,
then JIT). The lowering phase produces physical operator
*objects*; it does not generate any code. The objects expose
methods that the JIT calls.

**Memory allocation** belongs to setup-time bookkeeping in the
runtime, driven by physical operators but not allocated by the
lowering rules. The lowering rule says "this build operator will
need a hash map of size approximately N"; the runtime allocates
when the query starts.

**Parallelism decisions** also do not happen here. Whether to
parallelise the join across multiple worker threads is decided at
runtime by the task scheduler (Chapter 15), not at lowering time.

The lowering phase's scope is narrow: pick a class, instantiate it
with the right configuration, hand it to the next phase.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch10-summary}

The lowering phase rewrites a logical plan into a physical plan by
replacing each logical operator with one or more physical
operators. The dispatch is through a `LoweringRuleRegistry`,
selecting an implementation by name and (for joins) by trait.
Stateful operators (joins, aggregations) lower into a build/probe
pair that share state through an `OperatorHandlerId`. Stateless
operators lower one-to-one. The phase is small (about a dozen
rules) and largely mechanical; the interesting decisions —
physical join type, memory layout — were already made by the
optimiser.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch10-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 10.1: read a hash-join lowering"}
Set a breakpoint at the entry of the hash-join lowering rule.
Submit a hash-join query (any `JoinMultipleStreams.test` will
do). Inspect the lowered plan: confirm two physical operators
(`HJBuildPhysicalOperator`, `HJProbePhysicalOperator`) replaced
the single `JoinLogicalOperator`. What `OperatorHandlerId` was
chosen? How does it tie the two halves together?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 10.2: nested-loop fallback"}
From Chapter 9's exercise, you have a query with an inequality
join. Confirm that lowering produces `NLJBuildPhysicalOperator`
and `NLJProbePhysicalOperator`. Compare the runtime against the
hash-join case.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 10.3: implementation registration"}
Locate the line(s) that register the HashJoin and NLJoin
lowering rules in the registry. Compare to the registration
pattern for the source plugins (Chapter 8). Are they the same
mechanism? They should be — both use `LoweringRuleRegistry` /
`SourceRegistry` on top of the static-plugin-registry framework.
:::
